title: Linear Algebra Review, Part II
text: This note is a crash course in linear algebra in infinite dimensions: Hilbert spaces, bounded operators, the ways infinite dimensions differ from finite ones, compact operators, the spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators, and a brief look at unbounded operators such as the Laplacian. It assumes Part I, especially the variational proof of the spectral theorem (Part I, Section 2), which Section 7 below follows almost verbatim.

title: Linear Algebra Review, Part II
text:
Why we need it
Many objects in spectral ML are finite-dimensional samples of infinite-dimensional ones:

A kernel matrix \(K_{ij} = k(x_i, x_j)\) on \(m\) sample points approximates the integral operator \((T_k f)(x) = \int k(x, y) f(y)\, d\mu(y)\) on \(L^2(\mu)\).
A graph Laplacian built on points sampled from a manifold approximates the Laplace–Beltrami operator.
A graphon is the limit object of a sequence of dense graphs, and its adjacency “matrix” is an integral operator.
An infinite graph (a lattice, a tree) has an adjacency operator on \(\ell^2(V)\).

To ask whether the spectrum of the sample converges to the spectrum of the limit, we first need to know what the spectrum of the limit is. The good news: for the operators above that are compact and self-adjoint, the answer looks almost exactly like Part I, Theorem 2.2. The bad news: most other intuitions from finite dimensions fail. This part explains which ones and why.

title: Linear Algebra Review, Part II
text:
1. Normed spaces and completeness
A norm on a vector space \(X\) is a function \(\|\cdot\|: X \to [0,\infty)\) that is positive definite, homogeneous (\(\|cx\| = |c|\,\|x\|\)), and satisfies the triangle inequality. A normed space is a Banach space if it is complete: every Cauchy sequence converges.
Examples:

\(\ell^p = \{(x_k)_{k\ge1} : \sum_k |x_k|^p < \infty\}\) with \(\|x\|_p = (\sum_k |x_k|^p)^{1/p}\), for \(1 \le p < \infty\).
\(\ell^\infty\), the bounded sequences, with the sup norm.
\(C([0,1])\), the continuous functions, with \(\|f\|_\infty = \sup_t |f(t)|\).
\(L^p(\mu)\), the (equivalence classes of) measurable functions with \(\int |f|^p\, d\mu < \infty\).

Finite vs. infinite dimensions.

In finite dimensions, all norms are equivalent, every subspace is closed, and every linear map is continuous. None of these holds in infinite dimensions.
\(C([0,1])\) with the norm \(\|f\|_2 = (\int_0^1 |f|^2)^{1/2}\) is a normed space but not complete. Its completion is \(L^2([0,1])\). This is one reason \(L^2\), with its “functions defined only almost everywhere”, is the natural setting.
In infinite dimensions, “subspace” and “closed subspace” are different notions, and most theorems need the second. For instance, the finitely supported sequences \(c_{00} \subset \ell^2\) form a proper subspace that is dense: its closure is all of \(\ell^2\).

title: Linear Algebra Review, Part II
text:
2. Hilbert spaces
A Hilbert space \(H\) is an inner product space that is complete in the induced norm. Examples:

\(\mathbb{F}^n\).
\(\ell^2\) (or \(\ell^2(V)\) for a countable set \(V\)) with \(\langle x, y\rangle = \sum_k x_k \bar y_k\).
\(L^2(\mu)\) with \(\langle f, g\rangle = \int f \bar g\, d\mu\).
Reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS), which we will meet with kernel methods.

\(\ell^p\) and \(L^p\) for \(p \ne 2\) are Banach but not Hilbert spaces; their norms fail the parallelogram law.
Theorem 2.1 (Projection theorem). Let \(M \subseteq H\) be a closed subspace. Every \(x \in H\) has a unique nearest point \(P_M x \in M\), characterized by \(x - P_M x \perp M\). The map \(P_M\) is linear, \(P_M^2 = P_M = P_M^*\), and \(\|P_M\| \le 1\). Moreover, \(H = M \oplus M^\perp\) and \((M^\perp)^\perp = M\).
Proof sketch. Let \(d = \inf_{m \in M}\|x - m\|\) and pick \(m_k \in M\) with \(\|x - m_k\| \to d\). By the parallelogram law applied to \(x - m_j\) and \(x - m_k\), \[
\|m_j - m_k\|^2 = 2\|x-m_j\|^2 + 2\|x-m_k\|^2 - 4\big\|x - \tfrac{m_j+m_k}{2}\big\|^2 \le 2\|x-m_j\|^2 + 2\|x-m_k\|^2 - 4d^2 \to 0.
\] So \((m_k)\) is Cauchy. Completeness of \(H\) and closedness of \(M\) give a limit \(m_\star \in M\) with \(\|x - m_\star\| = d\). The orthogonality characterization follows from the same first-order argument as in Part I, Lemma 2.3. \(\blacksquare\)
Closedness is essential. For \(M = c_{00} \subset \ell^2\) we get \(M^\perp = \{0\}\), yet \(M \ne \ell^2\), so \(H \ne M \oplus M^\perp\).
Theorem 2.2 (Riesz representation). Every continuous linear functional \(\varphi : H \to \mathbb{F}\) has the form \(\varphi(x) = \langle x, y\rangle\) for a unique \(y \in H\), and \(\|\varphi\| = \|y\|\).
Proof sketch. If \(\varphi = 0\), take \(y = 0\). Otherwise \(\ker \varphi\) is a closed proper subspace, so by Theorem 2.1 there is a unit vector \(z \perp \ker\varphi\). For any \(x\), the vector \(\varphi(x) z - \varphi(z) x\) lies in \(\ker\varphi\) and is therefore orthogonal to \(z\). Expanding gives \(\varphi(x) = \langle x, \overline{\varphi(z)}\, z\rangle\). \(\blacksquare\)

4. Bounded operators and adjoints
For normed spaces \(X, Y\), a linear map \(T : X \to Y\) is bounded if \(\|T\| := \sup_{\|x\| \le 1}\|Tx\| < \infty\).
Proposition 4.1. A linear map is continuous iff it is continuous at \(0\) iff it is bounded.
In finite dimensions every linear map is bounded. In infinite dimensions this fails, and some of the most important operators, including differentiation and Laplacians, are unbounded. Section 8 discusses them. Until then, “operator” means bounded operator.
Let \(B(H)\) denote the bounded operators on a Hilbert space \(H\). For \(T \in B(H)\) and fixed \(y\), the functional \(x \mapsto \langle Tx, y\rangle\) is continuous. By Riesz, it equals \(\langle x, T^*y\rangle\) for a unique \(T^*y\). This defines the adjoint \(T^* \in B(H)\), with \(\|T^*\| = \|T\|\) and \(\|T^*T\| = \|T\|^2\). The definitions of self-adjoint, PSD, orthogonal projection (\(P = P^2 = P^*\)), and unitary (\(U^*U = UU^* = I\)) carry over unchanged, and Part I, Lemma 2.1 holds verbatim for self-adjoint \(T \in B(H)\) provided \(W\) is a closed invariant subspace.
A useful fact about self-adjoint operators, whose proof uses only the parallelogram law:
Lemma 4.2. If \(T \in B(H)\) is self-adjoint, then \(\|T\| = \sup_{\|x\|=1} |\langle Tx, x\rangle|\).
Proof. Let \(M\) denote the supremum. Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(M \le \|T\|\). For the reverse, expand using self-adjointness to get, for all \(x, y\), \[
4\,\mathrm{Re}\,\langle Tx, y\rangle = \langle T(x+y), x+y\rangle - \langle T(x-y), x-y\rangle \le M\big(\|x+y\|^2 + \|x-y\|^2\big) = 2M\big(\|x\|^2 + \|y\|^2\big).
\] For \(\|x\| = 1\) with \(Tx \ne 0\), put \(y = Tx/\|Tx\|\). The left side becomes \(4\|Tx\|\) and the right side \(4M\). So \(\|Tx\| \le M\). \(\blacksquare\)

title: Linear Algebra Review, Part II
section: 5. What goes wrong in infinite dimensions
text:
5. What goes wrong in infinite dimensions
Keep the following examples in mind. They are exactly what the compactness hypothesis in Section 7 rules out.
(a) Injective does not imply surjective. The right shift \(S(x_1, x_2, \dots) = (0, x_1, x_2, \dots)\) on \(\ell^2\) is an isometry (\(\|Sx\| = \|x\|\)), so it is injective, but it is not surjective. Its adjoint is the left shift \(S^*(x_1, x_2, \dots) = (x_2, x_3, \dots)\), which is surjective but not injective. There is no rank–nullity theorem.
(b) A self-adjoint operator may have no eigenvalues. Let \((Mf)(t) = t\,f(t)\) on \(L^2([0,1])\). Then \(M\) is bounded, self-adjoint, and PSD, with \(\|M\| = 1\). If \(Mf = \lambda f\), then \((t - \lambda) f(t) = 0\) almost everywhere, which forces \(f = 0\) in \(L^2\). So \(M\) has no eigenvectors at all. Yet \(M\) is clearly “diagonal” with “eigenvalues” \(t \in [0,1]\). It is diagonal in a continuous sense, with generalized eigenfunctions \(\delta_\lambda \notin L^2\). The right shift \(S\) also has no eigenvalues.
(c) The spectrum is more than the eigenvalues. For \(T \in B(H)\), define the spectrum \[
\sigma(T) = \{\lambda \in \mathbb{C} : T - \lambda I \text{ is not a bijection } H \to H\}.
\] (By the bounded inverse theorem, a bounded bijection automatically has a bounded inverse.) The set of eigenvalues, or point spectrum, is only a subset of \(\sigma(T)\). In example (b), \(\sigma(M) = [0,1]\), but \(M\) has no eigenvalues: \(M - \lambda I\) is injective but not surjective for \(\lambda \in [0,1]\).
Standard facts about the spectrum:

\(\sigma(T)\) is a nonempty compact subset of \(\mathbb{C}\) contained in \(\{|\lambda| \le \|T\|\}\).
If \(T\) is self-adjoint, then \(\sigma(T) \subseteq [m, M]\), where \(m = \inf_{\|x\|=1}\langle Tx, x\rangle\) and \(M = \sup_{\|x\|=1}\langle Tx, x\rangle\). Both \(m\) and \(M\) belong to \(\sigma(T)\).

In finite dimensions the spectrum is exactly the set of eigenvalues.
(d) The unit ball is not compact. An orthonormal sequence \((e_k)\) satisfies \(\|e_j - e_k\| = \sqrt 2\) for \(j \ne k\), so it has no convergent subsequence. This is exactly the step in Part I, Lemma 2.3 that fails: \(\sup_{\|x\|=1}\langle Tx, x\rangle\) need not be attained. In example (b), the supremum \(1\) is approached by functions concentrating near \(t = 1\) but never reached.
(e) Weak vs. strong convergence. A sequence \(x_k\) converges weakly to \(x\), written \(x_k \rightharpoonup x\), if \(\langle x_k, y\rangle \to \langle x, y\rangle\) for every \(y\). By Bessel’s inequality, every orthonormal sequence satisfies \(e_k \rightharpoonup 0\), even though \(\|e_k\| = 1\). Bounded sequences in a Hilbert space always have weakly convergent subsequences. The phenomenon in (d) is that weak limits can lose mass.

title: Linear Algebra Review, Part II
text:
6. Compact operators
Definition. \(T \in B(H)\) is compact if the image of every bounded sequence has a convergent subsequence. Equivalently, the closure of \(T(\text{unit ball})\) is compact.
A compact operator converts the weak convergence of Section 5(e) into norm convergence: if \(x_k \rightharpoonup x\), then \(Tx_k \to Tx\). Intuitively, a compact operator is one that is “almost finite-dimensional”.
Proposition 6.1.

Every finite-rank bounded operator (one with \(\dim \operatorname{range} T < \infty\)) is compact.
If \(T_n\) are compact and \(\|T_n - T\| \to 0\), then \(T\) is compact. Consequently, norm limits of finite-rank operators are compact. On a Hilbert space the converse also holds: every compact operator is such a limit.
If \(T\) is compact and \(A, B\) are bounded, then \(ATB\) is compact. \(T^*\) is compact iff \(T\) is.
On an infinite-dimensional \(H\), the identity operator is not compact (Section 5(d)). Hence a compact operator on an infinite-dimensional space is never invertible, and \(0 \in \sigma(T)\).

Proof of (2). Let \((x_k)\) be bounded by \(1\). By a diagonal argument, pass to a subsequence along which \((T_n x_k)_k\) converges for every \(n\). Then \[
\|Tx_j - Tx_k\| \le 2\|T - T_n\| + \|T_n x_j - T_n x_k\|.
\] Choose \(n\) so the first term is small, then take \(j, k\) large to make the second term small. So \((Tx_k)\) is Cauchy, hence convergent. \(\blacksquare\)
Examples.

Diagonal operators. For \(d = (d_k)\) bounded, \(D(x)_k = d_k x_k\) on \(\ell^2\) is compact iff \(d_k \to 0\). (If \(d_k \to 0\), the truncations are finite-rank approximations. If \(|d_k| \ge \delta\) infinitely often, the vectors \(De_k\) along those \(k\) are pairwise at distance \(\ge \sqrt2\,\delta\).) The multiplication operator \(M\) of Section 5(b) is not compact.
Hilbert–Schmidt integral operators. Let \((X, \mu)\) be a \(\sigma\)-finite measure space and \(K \in L^2(\mu \otimes \mu)\). Define \[
(T_K f)(x) = \int_X K(x,y)\, f(y)\, d\mu(y).
\] By Cauchy–Schwarz, \(|T_K f(x)|^2 \le \int |K(x,y)|^2 d\mu(y) \cdot \|f\|^2\). Integrating in \(x\) gives \(\|T_K\| \le \|K\|_{L^2(\mu\otimes\mu)}\). Finite sums \(\sum_i a_i(x) b_i(y)\) are dense in \(L^2(\mu \otimes\mu)\), and each such kernel gives a finite-rank operator. So \(T_K\) is a norm limit of finite-rank operators, hence compact. It is self-adjoint iff \(K(x,y) = \overline{K(y,x)}\) almost everywhere. Every kernel-method integral operator and every graphon operator is of this form.

title: Linear Algebra Review, Part II
section: 7. The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators
text:
7. The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators
Throughout, \(H \ne \{0\}\) is a Hilbert space over \(\mathbb{F}\) and \(T \in B(H)\) is compact and self-adjoint.

7.1 Statement
Theorem 7.1 (Spectral theorem, compact self-adjoint operators). There exist a finite or countably infinite orthonormal sequence \((e_k)\) in \(H\) and nonzero real numbers \((\lambda_k)\) with \(|\lambda_1| \ge |\lambda_2| \ge \cdots\) such that:

\(T e_k = \lambda_k e_k\) for every \(k\).
If the sequence is infinite, then \(\lambda_k \to 0\).
For every \(x \in H\), \[
Tx = \sum_k \lambda_k \langle x, e_k\rangle\, e_k,
\] with convergence in operator norm: \(\big\|T - \sum_{k \le n}\lambda_k e_k e_k^*\big\| = |\lambda_{n+1}| \to 0\).
\(H = \ker T \oplus \overline{\operatorname{span}}\{e_k\}\), an orthogonal direct sum.
The nonzero eigenvalues of \(T\) are exactly the \(\lambda_k\). Each has finite multiplicity, and its eigenspace is spanned by the \(e_k\) with \(\lambda_k\) equal to it.

In particular, if \(H\) is separable, then combining \((e_k)\) with an orthonormal basis of \(\ker T\) gives an orthonormal basis of \(H\) consisting of eigenvectors of \(T\).
Compare with Part I, Theorem 2.2. The only new features are that there may be infinitely many eigenvalues, that they can accumulate only at \(0\), and that \(\ker T\) may be infinite-dimensional. The spectrum is \(\sigma(T) = \{\lambda_k\} \cup \{0\}\) when \(H\) is infinite-dimensional.


7.2 The key lemma: the top eigenvalue exists
In Part I, Lemma 2.3, compactness of the unit sphere guaranteed that the maximum of the Rayleigh quotient is attained. Here, compactness of \(T\) plays that role.
Lemma 7.2. If \(T\) is compact and self-adjoint, then \(\|T\|\) or \(-\|T\|\) is an eigenvalue of \(T\).
Proof. If \(T = 0\), every nonzero vector is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(0\). Assume \(T \ne 0\). By Lemma 4.2 there are unit vectors \(x_n\) with \(|\langle Tx_n, x_n\rangle| \to \|T\|\). These numbers are real, so passing to a subsequence we may assume \(\langle Tx_n, x_n\rangle \to \lambda\), where \(\lambda \in \{\|T\|, -\|T\|\}\) and \(\lambda \ne 0\). Then \[
\|Tx_n - \lambda x_n\|^2 = \|Tx_n\|^2 - 2\lambda\langle Tx_n, x_n\rangle + \lambda^2 \le 2\lambda^2 - 2\lambda \langle Tx_n, x_n\rangle \longrightarrow 0,
\] using \(\|Tx_n\| \le \|T\| = |\lambda|\). By compactness, a further subsequence has \(Tx_n \to y\) for some \(y\). Then \(\lambda x_n = Tx_n - (Tx_n - \lambda x_n) \to y\), so \(x_n \to y/\lambda\) and \(\|y\| = |\lambda| \ne 0\). By continuity of \(T\), \[
Ty = \lim_n T(\lambda x_n) = \lambda \lim_n Tx_n = \lambda y. \qquad\blacksquare
\]
The first display is the same “approximate eigenvector” computation behind Part I, Lemma 2.3. Compactness upgrades an approximate eigenvector to a genuine one. Without compactness this fails: for the operator \(M\) of Section 5(b), such approximate eigenvectors exist for every \(\lambda \in [0,1]\), but no genuine eigenvector does.


7.3 Proof of Theorem 7.1
Construction. Set \(H_1 = H\). We build \(e_1, e_2, \dots\) inductively. Suppose \(e_1, \dots, e_{n-1}\) have been constructed, with \(Te_k = \lambda_k e_k\), and let \[
H_n = \{e_1, \dots, e_{n-1}\}^\perp.
\] This is a closed subspace, hence a Hilbert space. It is \(T\)-invariant: if \(x \perp e_k\) for all \(k < n\), then \(\langle Tx, e_k\rangle = \langle x, Te_k\rangle = \lambda_k\langle x, e_k\rangle = 0\). The restriction \(T_n = T|_{H_n}\) is therefore compact and self-adjoint on \(H_n\).

If \(T_n = 0\) (this includes the case \(H_n = \{0\}\)), stop. The sequence is finite, of length \(n - 1\).
Otherwise, Lemma 7.2 gives a unit vector \(e_n \in H_n\) with \(Te_n = \lambda_n e_n\) and \(|\lambda_n| = \|T_n\| > 0\).

Since \(H_{n+1} \subseteq H_n\), we have \(|\lambda_{n+1}| = \|T_{n+1}\| \le \|T_n\| = |\lambda_n|\). By construction the \(e_k\) are orthonormal. This proves (1).
(2) The eigenvalues tend to \(0\). Suppose the sequence is infinite and \(|\lambda_k| \ge \delta > 0\) for all \(k\). Then for \(j \ne k\), \[
\|Te_j - Te_k\|^2 = \lambda_j^2 + \lambda_k^2 \ge 2\delta^2,
\] so \((Te_k)\) has no convergent subsequence even though \((e_k)\) is bounded. This contradicts compactness.
(3) The expansion. Fix \(x\) and let \(P_n x = \sum_{k \le n}\langle x, e_k\rangle e_k\). Then \(x - P_n x \in H_{n+1}\) and \(\|x - P_n x\| \le \|x\|\). Since \(T P_n x = \sum_{k\le n}\lambda_k \langle x, e_k\rangle e_k\), \[
\Big\|Tx - \sum_{k\le n}\lambda_k\langle x, e_k\rangle e_k\Big\| = \|T_{n+1}(x - P_nx)\| \le |\lambda_{n+1}|\,\|x\|.
\] If the sequence stops at \(N\), set \(\lambda_{N+1} := 0\) (because \(T_{N+1} = 0\)). In either case the right side tends to \(0\) by (2). This proves the pointwise expansion and the operator-norm bound \(\le |\lambda_{n+1}|\). Equality follows by testing on \(x = e_{n+1}\).
(4) The kernel. If \(x \perp e_k\) for all \(k\), then (3) gives \(Tx = 0\). Conversely, if \(Tx = 0\), then \(\langle x, e_k\rangle = \lambda_k^{-1}\langle x, Te_k\rangle = \lambda_k^{-1}\langle Tx, e_k\rangle = 0\). Hence \(\ker T = \{e_k\}^\perp\). Since \(\{e_k\}^\perp = \big(\overline{\operatorname{span}}\{e_k\}\big)^\perp\), Theorem 2.1 gives \(H = \ker T \oplus \overline{\operatorname{span}}\{e_k\}\).
(5) No other nonzero eigenvalues, and finite multiplicity. Let \(Tx = \mu x\) with \(\mu \ne 0\) and \(x \neq 0\). By (4), write \(x = x_0 + \sum_k \langle x, e_k\rangle e_k\) with \(x_0 \in \ker T\). Applying \(T\) and using (3), \[
\mu x_0 + \sum_k \mu\langle x, e_k\rangle e_k = \sum_k \lambda_k\langle x, e_k\rangle e_k.
\] Comparing components gives \(x_0 = 0\) and \(\langle x, e_k\rangle = 0\) whenever \(\lambda_k \ne \mu\). Since \(x \ne 0\), some \(\lambda_k\) equals \(\mu\), and \(x\) lies in the span of \(\{e_k : \lambda_k = \mu\}\). That set is finite because \(\lambda_k \to 0\) and \(\mu \ne 0\).
Separable case. \(\ker T\) is a closed subspace of a separable Hilbert space, so it has a countable orthonormal basis. Its union with \((e_k)\) is orthonormal (by (4)) and has dense span (by (4)), so it is an orthonormal basis of \(H\) by Theorem 3.1. \(\blacksquare\)


7.4 Consequences and extensions
Min–max for compact operators. Order the positive eigenvalues as \(\lambda_1^+ \ge \lambda_2^+ \ge \dots > 0\), with multiplicity. If there are at least \(k\) of them, then \[
\lambda_k^+ = \max_{\dim S = k}\ \min_{x \in S\setminus\{0\}} R_T(x),
\] by the same proof as Part I, Theorem 2.8. The analogous formula holds for the negative eigenvalues. Weyl’s inequality (Part I, Corollary 2.9) also carries over. This is the basic tool for comparing the spectrum of a kernel matrix with that of its limiting integral operator.
Functional calculus. For bounded \(f\) with \(f(0) = 0\), the operator \(f(T) = \sum_k f(\lambda_k)\, e_k e_k^*\) is well defined. With \(f(0)\) arbitrary, add \(f(0)\) times the projection onto \(\ker T\).
Mercer’s theorem. Let \(X\) be a compact metric space and \(\mu\) a finite Borel measure with full support. Let \(k\) be a continuous, symmetric, positive semidefinite kernel, meaning every Gram matrix \([k(x_i,x_j)]\) is PSD. Then \(T_k\) is compact, self-adjoint, and PSD on \(L^2(\mu)\). Its eigenfunctions \(\varphi_k\) for positive eigenvalues can be chosen continuous, and \[
k(x,y) = \sum_k \lambda_k\, \varphi_k(x)\,\overline{\varphi_k(y)},
\] with absolute and uniform convergence on \(X \times X\). Consequently, \(\sum_k \lambda_k = \int k(x,x)\, d\mu(x) < \infty\), i.e., \(T_k\) is trace class. The map \(x \mapsto (\sqrt{\lambda_k}\,\varphi_k(x))_k \in \ell^2\) is an explicit feature map for \(k\).
Beyond compact operators. Every bounded self-adjoint operator admits a spectral theorem, but in general it is unitarily equivalent to a multiplication operator like \(M\) in Section 5(b) on some \(L^2(\nu)\), not to a diagonal matrix. Equivalently, it has a projection-valued spectral measure. The spectrum then splits into a discrete part (isolated eigenvalues of finite multiplicity) and an essential part. For compact operators the essential spectrum is at most \(\{0\}\). The essential spectrum is what makes, for instance, the unnormalized graph Laplacian’s spectral clustering inconsistent in some regimes (von Luxburg–Belkin–Bousquet). See Reed & Simon Vol. I or Teschl for the general theory.

title: Linear Algebra Review, Part II
text:
8. Unbounded operators
There are two quite different kinds of unbounded linear operators. Only the second kind matters in practice.
(i) Everywhere-defined but discontinuous maps. Every infinite-dimensional normed space \(X\) carries linear maps \(T : X \to X\) (or linear functionals \(X \to \mathbb{F}\)) that are defined on all of \(X\) but are not bounded.
Construction:

Pick linearly independent unit vectors \(b_1, b_2, \dots\).
Extend them to a Hamel basis of \(X\). This uses Zorn’s lemma.
Set \(f(b_k) = k\), set \(f = 0\) on the remaining basis vectors, and extend linearly.

Then \(|f(b_k)|/\|b_k\| = k \to \infty\). Such maps are pathological: they cannot be written down explicitly, and their graphs are not closed. By the closed graph theorem, an everywhere-defined linear map between Banach spaces with a closed graph is automatically bounded. These maps never arise in applications, and we will not see them again.
(ii) Densely defined operators. The unbounded operators of analysis are defined only on a dense subspace \(\operatorname{dom}(T) \subsetneq H\), called the domain. Examples:

Diagonal operator on \(\ell^2\): \((Tx)_k = k\,x_k\), with \(\operatorname{dom}(T) = \{x : \sum_k k^2|x_k|^2 < \infty\}\). The domain contains \(c_{00}\), so it is dense, and \(\|Te_k\| = k\).
Differentiation on \(L^2([0,1])\): \(Tf = f'\), with domain, say, \(C^1([0,1])\) or the Sobolev space \(H^1\). Since \(T e^{2\pi i k t} = 2\pi i k\, e^{2\pi i k t}\), \(T\) has no finite norm.
Multiplication by \(t\) on \(L^2(\mathbb{R})\): \(\operatorname{dom} = \{f : tf \in L^2\}\). This is the unbounded cousin of the operator \(M\) in Section 5(b).
The Laplace–Beltrami operator \(\Delta\) on \(L^2\) of a Riemannian manifold. This is the continuum limit of graph Laplacians built on sampled points.
The graph Laplacian of an infinite graph with unbounded degrees, acting on \(\ell^2(V)\). For bounded degree \(d_{\max}\), one has \(\|L\| \le 2d_{\max}\), so \(L\) is bounded. Without a degree bound, \(\|L\delta_u\| \ge d_u\) is unbounded.

Symmetry forces unboundedness to live on a proper domain.
Theorem 8.1 (Hellinger–Toeplitz). If \(T : H \to H\) is linear, defined on all of \(H\), and symmetric (\(\langle Tx, y\rangle = \langle x, Ty\rangle\) for all \(x, y\)), then \(T\) is bounded.
Proof. We check that the graph of \(T\) is closed. Suppose \(x_n \to x\) and \(Tx_n \to y\). For every \(z\), \[
\langle y, z\rangle = \lim_n \langle Tx_n, z\rangle = \lim_n \langle x_n, Tz\rangle = \langle x, Tz\rangle = \langle Tx, z\rangle,
\] so \(y = Tx\). The closed graph theorem then gives boundedness. \(\blacksquare\)
So an unbounded “self-adjoint” operator like \(\Delta\) cannot be defined on all of \(L^2\). The domain is part of the data.
Symmetric vs. self-adjoint. For densely defined \(T\), the adjoint \(T^*\) is defined on \[
\operatorname{dom}(T^*) = \{y : x \mapsto \langle Tx, y\rangle \text{ is bounded on } \operatorname{dom}(T)\},
\] with \(T^*y\) given by Riesz representation. Two notions separate:

\(T\) is symmetric if \(\langle Tx, y\rangle = \langle x, Ty\rangle\) for all \(x, y \in \operatorname{dom}(T)\), i.e., \(T^*\) extends \(T\).
\(T\) is self-adjoint if \(T = T^*\), including equality of domains.

In finite dimensions, and for bounded operators, the two notions coincide. Here they do not, and the difference is real.
Example. \(T = -\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\) on \(C_c^\infty((0,1))\) is symmetric but not self-adjoint. It has several self-adjoint extensions, corresponding to boundary conditions, and they have different spectra:

Dirichlet, \(f(0) = f(1) = 0\): eigenvalues \((k\pi)^2\) for \(k \ge 1\), eigenfunctions \(\sin(k\pi x)\).
Neumann, \(f'(0) = f'(1) = 0\): eigenvalues \((k\pi)^2\) for \(k \ge 0\), eigenfunctions \(\cos(k\pi x)\).

The same phenomenon appears for Laplacians on non-compact manifolds and on some infinite graphs. Whether the Laplacian is essentially self-adjoint (has a unique self-adjoint extension) is a genuine question there; see Grigor’yan or Schmüdgen. For a self-adjoint unbounded operator, the spectrum is still real and closed, but it is unbounded. A spectral theorem holds in the multiplication-operator form of Section 7.4.
Taming unbounded operators with compact resolvents. The standard way to bring unbounded operators within reach of Section 7 is to invert them. Suppose \(T \succeq 0\) is self-adjoint and its resolvent \((I + T)^{-1}\) is compact. The resolvent is then bounded, self-adjoint, and injective. Theorem 7.1 gives an orthonormal eigenbasis \((e_k)\) of \(H\) with \((I+T)^{-1}e_k = \nu_k e_k\) and \(\nu_k \downarrow 0\). Hence \[
T e_k = \mu_k e_k, \qquad \mu_k = \nu_k^{-1} - 1, \qquad 0 \le \mu_1 \le \mu_2 \le \dots \to \infty.
\] This is exactly the spectral picture of the Laplacian on a compact manifold: a discrete spectrum going to infinity, and an \(L^2\) eigenbasis.
Concrete instance. For the Dirichlet Laplacian \(T = -\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\) on \([0,1]\), \(T\) itself is invertible. Its inverse is the integral operator with the Green’s function \[
G(x,y) = \min(x,y) - xy,
\] a continuous symmetric kernel, so \(T^{-1}\) is a compact Hilbert–Schmidt operator (Section 6). Compare Exercise 4, where \(\min(x,y)\) plays the same role for mixed boundary conditions.
Why this matters in the course.

Graph Laplacians on \(m\) sampled points converge to \(\Delta\), an unbounded operator. So spectral convergence results (Belkin–Niyogi, García Trillos et al.) are stated eigenvalue-by-eigenvalue, or through bounded functions of the operator.
Diffusion maps work with the heat semigroup \(e^{-t\Delta} = \sum_k e^{-t\mu_k} e_k e_k^*\). For \(t > 0\), this is a bounded, compact, self-adjoint operator, even though \(\Delta\) is not.
Passing to a bounded function of an unbounded operator — resolvent, heat semigroup, or spectral projection — is the recurring technique.

title: The Davis–Kahan sin Θ Theorem
text:
Weyl’s inequality (Review Part I, Corollary 2.9) says that eigenvalues of a self-adjoint matrix move by at most \(\|E\|\) under a perturbation \(E\). Eigenvectors are more fragile. If two eigenvalues are close, an arbitrarily small perturbation can rotate the corresponding eigenvectors by \(90°\). The Davis–Kahan theorem says this is the only obstruction: an invariant subspace is stable, with error controlled by \(\|E\|\) divided by the eigengap separating it from the rest of the spectrum.
Notation follows Part I of the review: \(\mathbb{F} \in \{\mathbb{R}, \mathbb{C}\}\), \(M^*\) is the conjugate transpose, and \(\|\cdot\|\) is the operator (spectral) norm unless marked otherwise.

title: The Davis–Kahan sin Θ Theorem
text:
1. Motivating example
Let \(A = \operatorname{diag}(1+\varepsilon, 1)\) and \(\hat A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 + \varepsilon/2 & \varepsilon/2 \\ \varepsilon/2 & 1 + \varepsilon/2\end{pmatrix}\).

The top eigenvector of \(A\) is \(e_1\).
The top eigenvector of \(\hat A\) is \((e_1 + e_2)/\sqrt2\).
The perturbation \(\hat A - A = \frac{\varepsilon}{2}\begin{pmatrix}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}\) has norm \(\varepsilon/\sqrt2\), which is tiny.
Yet the top eigenvector rotated by \(45°\).

The perturbation is on the same scale as the eigengap \(\varepsilon\), so no eigenvector stability can be expected. By contrast, the two-dimensional eigenspace \(\operatorname{span}\{e_1, e_2\}\) did not move at all.
Lesson: bound the distance between subspaces, and measure the perturbation relative to the gap.

title: The Davis–Kahan sin Θ Theorem
text:
2. Distances between subspaces
Let \(V, \hat V \in \mathbb{F}^{n\times k}\) have orthonormal columns (\(V^*V = \hat V^*\hat V = I_k\)), spanning subspaces \(\mathcal V\) and \(\hat{\mathcal V}\).
Principal angles. The singular values of \(\hat V^* V \in \mathbb{F}^{k\times k}\) lie in \([0,1]\). Write them as \(\cos\theta_1 \ge \dots \ge \cos\theta_k\), with \(\theta_i \in [0, \pi/2]\). The \(\theta_i\) are the principal angles between \(\mathcal V\) and \(\hat{\mathcal V}\). They do not depend on the choice of orthonormal bases. Set \[
\sin\Theta(V, \hat V) = \operatorname{diag}(\sin\theta_1, \dots, \sin\theta_k).
\]
Lemma 2.1. Let \(\hat V_\perp \in \mathbb{F}^{n\times(n-k)}\) complete \(\hat V\) to a unitary matrix \([\hat V\ \hat V_\perp]\).

The singular values of \(\hat V_\perp^* V\) are \(\sin\theta_1, \dots, \sin\theta_k\), padded with zeros if \(n - k > k\).
\(\|VV^* - \hat V \hat V^*\| = \|\sin\Theta\| = \sin\theta_1\), and \(\|VV^* - \hat V\hat V^*\|_F = \sqrt2\,\|\sin\Theta\|_F\).
There is a unitary \(O \in \mathbb{F}^{k\times k}\) with \(\|\hat V O - V\|_F \le \sqrt2\,\|\sin\Theta\|_F\).

Proof. (1) Since \(\hat V\hat V^* + \hat V_\perp \hat V_\perp^* = I\), \[
I_k = V^*V = (\hat V^*V)^*(\hat V^*V) + (\hat V_\perp^* V)^*(\hat V_\perp^* V).
\] So the eigenvalues of \((\hat V_\perp^*V)^*(\hat V_\perp^*V)\) are \(1 - \cos^2\theta_i = \sin^2\theta_i\).

In the orthonormal basis \([\hat V\ \hat V_\perp]\), a direct computation from (1) shows that \(VV^* - \hat V\hat V^*\) has eigenvalues \(\pm\sin\theta_i\), plus zeros. Both identities follow. (Exercise: carry out the \(2\times 2\) block computation.)
Take an SVD \(\hat V^*V = U (\cos\Theta) W^*\) and set \(O = UW^*\). Then \[
\|\hat VO - V\|_F^2 = 2k - 2\,\mathrm{Re}\operatorname{tr}(O^*\hat V^*V) = 2\sum_i (1 - \cos\theta_i) \le 2\sum_i \sin^2\theta_i,
\] using \(1 - c \le 1 - c^2\) for \(c \in [0,1]\). \(\blacksquare\)

Part (3) is what spectral clustering needs. The embedding computed from data, the rows of \(\hat V\), matches the ideal embedding (the rows of \(V\)) up to a rotation \(O\). A rotation does not affect \(k\)-means, since it preserves all pairwise distances.

title: The Davis–Kahan sin Θ Theorem
text:
3. The theorem
Theorem 3.1 (Davis–Kahan \(\sin\Theta\) theorem). Let \(A\) and \(\hat A = A + E\) be self-adjoint \(n\times n\) matrices.

Let \(V \in \mathbb{F}^{n\times k}\) have orthonormal columns with \(AV = V\Lambda_1\), where \(\Lambda_1\) is diagonal with entries in an interval \([a, b]\).
Let \(\hat V_\perp \in \mathbb{F}^{n\times(n-k)}\) have orthonormal columns with \(\hat A \hat V_\perp = \hat V_\perp \hat\Lambda_2\), where \(\hat\Lambda_2\) is diagonal with every entry outside \((a - \delta, b + \delta)\), for some \(\delta > 0\).

Let \(\hat V\) be the orthonormal complement of \(\hat V_\perp\). It spans the remaining \(k\) eigenvectors of \(\hat A\). Then for the operator norm and for the Frobenius norm, \[
\|\sin\Theta(V, \hat V)\| \;\le\; \frac{\|EV\|}{\delta} \;\le\; \frac{\|E\|}{\delta},
\qquad
\|\sin\Theta(V, \hat V)\|_F \;\le\; \frac{\|EV\|_F}{\delta}.
\]
In words: if the unperturbed eigenvalues of interest sit in \([a,b]\), and the perturbed eigenvalues we discard stay at distance \(\delta\) from that interval, then the subspace moves by at most \(\|E\|/\delta\).

3.1 The Sylvester lemma
Lemma 3.2. Let \(\Lambda \in \mathbb{F}^{k\times k}\) and \(D \in \mathbb{F}^{m\times m}\) be self-adjoint. Suppose the eigenvalues of \(\Lambda\) lie in \([a,b]\) and those of \(D\) lie outside \((a - \delta, b+\delta)\). Then for every \(X \in \mathbb{F}^{m\times k}\) and \(\|\cdot\| \in \{\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}}, \|\cdot\|_F\}\), \[
\|DX - X\Lambda\| \ge \delta\,\|X\|.
\]
Proof. Let \(c = (a+b)/2\) and \(r = (b-a)/2\). Then \(\|\Lambda - cI\| \le r\). Every eigenvalue of \(D - cI\) has absolute value at least \(r + \delta\), so \(D - cI\) is invertible with \(\|(D - cI)^{-1}\| \le 1/(r+\delta)\).
Set \(Y = DX - X\Lambda = (D - cI)X - X(\Lambda - cI)\). Then \(X = (D-cI)^{-1}\big(Y + X(\Lambda - cI)\big)\). Using \(\|PQ\| \le \|P\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|Q\|\) and \(\|QP\| \le \|Q\|\,\|P\|_{\mathrm{op}}\), which hold for both norms, \[
\|X\| \le \frac{\|Y\| + r\|X\|}{r + \delta}.
\] Rearranging gives \(\delta\|X\| \le \|Y\|\). \(\blacksquare\)
The centering trick is what makes the lemma work in operator norm. For the Frobenius norm alone there is a one-line proof when \(D\) and \(\Lambda\) are diagonal: \((DX - X\Lambda)_{ij} = (d_i - \lambda_j)X_{ij}\) and \(|d_i - \lambda_j| \ge \delta\).


3.2 Proof of Theorem 3.1
Let \(X = \hat V_\perp^* V\). By Lemma 2.1(1), \(\|X\| = \|\sin\Theta\|\) and \(\|X\|_F = \|\sin\Theta\|_F\). Multiply the identity \(\hat A V - V\Lambda_1 = (A + E)V - V\Lambda_1 = EV\) on the left by \(\hat V_\perp^*\), and use \(\hat V_\perp^*\hat A = \hat\Lambda_2\hat V_\perp^*\) (valid because \(\hat A\) is self-adjoint). This gives the Sylvester equation \[
\hat\Lambda_2 X - X\Lambda_1 = \hat V_\perp^* E V.
\] By Lemma 3.2, \(\delta\|X\| \le \|\hat V_\perp^* EV\| \le \|EV\|\). \(\blacksquare\)
The whole proof is two lines once the Sylvester equation is written down. The eigengap enters only through Lemma 3.2.


3.3 A version with the gap measured on \(A\) alone
In applications, \(A\) is an idealized (population) matrix whose spectrum we know, and \(\hat A\) is observed. The natural gap is that of \(A\). For the top-\(k\) eigenspace, let \[
\delta_0 = \lambda_k(A) - \lambda_{k+1}(A) > 0,
\] where \(\lambda_1(\cdot) \ge \dots \ge \lambda_n(\cdot)\).
Corollary 3.3. Let \(V\) and \(\hat V\) span the top-\(k\) eigenspaces of \(A\) and \(\hat A = A + E\). Then \[
\|\sin\Theta(V,\hat V)\| \le \frac{2\|E\|}{\delta_0}, \qquad \|\sin\Theta(V, \hat V)\|_F \le \frac{2\sqrt k\,\|E\|}{\delta_0}.
\]
Proof. Suppose first \(\|E\| \le \delta_0/2\). Apply Theorem 3.1 with \([a,b] = [\lambda_k(A), \lambda_1(A)]\). By Weyl, every discarded eigenvalue of \(\hat A\) satisfies \(\lambda_j(\hat A) \le \lambda_{k+1}(A) + \|E\| = a - (\delta_0 - \|E\|)\). So \(\delta = \delta_0 - \|E\| \ge \delta_0/2\) works.
If instead \(\|E\| > \delta_0/2\), the operator-norm bound exceeds \(1 \ge \|\sin\Theta\|\), so it holds trivially.
The Frobenius bound follows from \(\|\sin\Theta\|_F \le \sqrt k\,\|\sin\Theta\|\). \(\blacksquare\)
Yu, Wang & Samworth (2015) prove the sharper \(\|\sin\Theta\|_F \le 2\min(\sqrt k\,\|E\|, \|E\|_F)/\delta_0\) and handle eigenvalues in the middle of the spectrum, not just the top \(k\). Combined with Lemma 2.1(3), for some unitary \(O\), \[
\|\hat VO - V\|_F \le \frac{2\sqrt{2k}\,\|E\|}{\delta_0}.
\]

section: 4. Application sketch: why spectral clustering works
text:
4. Application sketch: why spectral clustering works
This is the template shared by Ng–Jordan–Weiss, the analysis in von Luxburg’s tutorial, and the stochastic block model analyses of Rohe–Chatterjee–Yu and Lei–Rinaldo.

Ideal matrix. Take \(k\) clusters with no edges between them, or a population matrix \(A = \mathbb{E}[\hat A]\) with block structure. Then the top-\(k\) eigenvectors of the appropriate matrix have rows that take only \(k\) distinct values, one per cluster.

Unnormalized block model: node \(i\) in cluster \(j\) has row \(\propto e_j^\top/\sqrt{n_j}\), up to a rotation.
Normalized Laplacian (Ng–Jordan–Weiss): rows are rescaled by the square roots of the degrees. After row-normalization, they become \(k\) mutually orthogonal unit vectors.

Let \(\Delta\) be the minimum distance between distinct rows.
Eigengap. Compute or lower-bound \(\delta_0 = \lambda_k(A) - \lambda_{k+1}(A)\). For a disconnected ideal graph, this is controlled by the spectral gaps of the individual clusters.
Perturbation size. Bound \(\|E\| = \|\hat A - A\|\). In the deterministic setting, \(E\) is the between-cluster weight. In the random setting, a matrix concentration inequality gives \(\|E\| = O(\sqrt{\text{max expected degree}})\) with high probability.
Davis–Kahan. \(\|\hat VO - V\|_F \le 2\sqrt{2k}\,\|E\|/\delta_0\).
Rounding. Call node \(i\) bad if its row satisfies \(\|(\hat VO)_i - V_i\| \ge \Delta/2\). By Markov’s inequality on the squared row errors, \[
\#\text{bad nodes} \le \frac{4\,\|\hat VO - V\|_F^2}{\Delta^2} \le \frac{32\,k\,\|E\|^2}{\Delta^2\,\delta_0^2}.
\] Assigning each good node to the nearest true center labels it correctly. For the centers found by (approximate) \(k\)-means, an extra argument is needed, which loses constant factors (Lei & Rinaldo 2015, Lemma 5.3).

The row-wise conclusion in step 5 comes from a Frobenius bound via Markov. Bounding every row individually needs \(\ell_{2\to\infty}\) or entrywise perturbation theory (Cape–Tang–Priebe; Abbe–Fan–Wang–Zhong), which is a natural “further directions” pointer.

section: 5. Sources and how they fit together
text:
5. Sources and how they fit together
Notes for planning the lecture. Titles, venues, and years are from memory. The Ng–Jordan–Weiss citation of Stewart & Sun in particular should be checked before it goes on a syllabus.
The original theorem.

C. Davis & W. M. Kahan, “The rotation of eigenvectors by a perturbation. III,” SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 7 (1970). The source of the \(\sin\Theta\), \(\tan\Theta\), \(\sin 2\Theta\) family of theorems, stated for operators on Hilbert space. Heavy going; better cited than assigned.
G. W. Stewart & J.-G. Sun, Matrix Perturbation Theory (Academic Press, 1990). The standard matrix-analysis reference for invariant-subspace perturbation. This is what Ng–Jordan–Weiss cite.
R. Bhatia, Matrix Analysis (GTM 169), Ch. VII. Clean proofs of the \(\sin\Theta\) theorems via Sylvester equations, including the operator-norm subtleties. The proof above follows this route.

Ng, Jordan & Weiss — the classical application. “On Spectral Clustering: Analysis and an Algorithm” (NIPS 2001).

Introduces the now-standard algorithm: normalized affinity \(D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}\), top-\(k\) eigenvectors, row-normalization, \(k\)-means.
The analysis treats the observed affinity matrix as a perturbation of the ideal block-diagonal one. It applies a Stewart–Sun subspace bound (a Davis–Kahan \(\sin\Theta\) theorem, not cited under that name) with an eigengap supplied by assumptions (A1)–(A4) on within-cluster connectivity and between-cluster weight.
Conclusion: the row-normalized embedding clusters tightly around \(k\) mutually orthogonal points.
Row-normalization is exactly what makes the ideal rows orthogonal unit vectors despite degree heterogeneity.
Good for the lecture as the historical origin. The assumptions are somewhat opaque, so a cleaner restatement is worth doing in class.

von Luxburg, “A Tutorial on Spectral Clustering,” Statistics and Computing (2007).

The perturbation-theory section states Davis–Kahan explicitly and explains why the eigengap between \(\lambda_k\) and \(\lambda_{k+1}\) is the right quantity.
Also discusses when the argument is shaky: the ideal eigenvectors must be piecewise constant, and the perturbation must be small in operator norm.
Probably the easiest version to present, and a good reading assignment.

Stochastic block model analyses — the modern template.

Rohe, Chatterjee & Yu, “Spectral clustering and the high-dimensional stochastic blockmodel,” Annals of Statistics (2011). Normalized Laplacian under the SBM, with the number of clusters allowed to grow. Uses concentration + Davis–Kahan + counting misclustered nodes.
Lei & Rinaldo, “Consistency of spectral clustering in stochastic block models,” Annals of Statistics (2015). Sharper, cleaner version for the adjacency matrix. Includes the approximate-\(k\)-means rounding lemma used in step 5 above. Best source for a complete, rigorous end-to-end proof.

Yu, Wang & Samworth, “A useful variant of the Davis–Kahan theorem for statisticians,” Biometrika (2015).

Requires an eigengap only for the population matrix \(A\), not for the noisy \(\hat A\). This is exactly what applications need, since the observed spectrum is not under our control.
Also gives the \(\min(\sqrt k\|E\|, \|E\|_F)\) form, and a version for singular vectors (Wedin-type).
Short, and a good reading.

Peng, Sun & Zanetti, “Partitioning well-clustered graphs: spectral clustering works!” (COLT 2015; journal version in SIAM J. Comput.).

A contrasting, worst-case (non-probabilistic) approach. Assumes a gap between \(\lambda_{k+1}\) of the normalized Laplacian and the \(k\)-way expansion constant \(\rho(k)\).
Proves a structure theorem: the bottom-\(k\) eigenvectors are close to cluster indicator vectors, and vice versa. This is argued directly, not through a black-box Davis–Kahan bound.
Connects naturally to the higher-order Cheeger inequality (Lee–Oveis Gharan–Trevisan) and fits a course with a spectral graph theory emphasis.
Useful to contrast with the Davis–Kahan route: which quantity plays the role of the eigengap, and why.

Further directions (row-wise / entrywise control).

Cape, Tang & Priebe, “The two-to-infinity norm and singular subspace geometry…,” Annals of Statistics (2019).
Abbe, Fan, Wang & Zhong, “Entrywise eigenvector analysis of random matrices with low expected rank,” Annals of Statistics (2020).
These give per-row bounds, and hence exact recovery results, where Davis–Kahan plus Markov only bounds the number of misclustered nodes.

Suggested lecture arc.

Motivating example (Section 1).
Principal angles (Section 2).
Davis–Kahan proof via the Sylvester equation (Section 3).
Ng–Jordan–Weiss as the historical application.
The clean five-step template (Section 4), with Lei–Rinaldo as the rigorous version.
Peng–Sun–Zanetti as the graph-theoretic alternative.
Pointer to entrywise theory.

Assign von Luxburg plus Yu–Wang–Samworth as reading.

Spectral methods are a powerful tool for understanding complex systems by studying the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of associated linear operators. Because their theory generalizes from finite-dimensional linear algebra to infinite-dimensional settings, they provide a unifying framework for the analysis and computation of a wide range of problems.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Eigenvectors, Eigenvalues and Diagonalization
Definition: An eigenvector of a matrix \(A\) is a nonzero vector \(\mathbf{v}\) such that
\[
A \mathbf{v} = \lambda \mathbf{v}
\] for some scalar \(\lambda\), called the eigenvalue corresponding to \(\mathbf{v}\).
Spectral Decomposition: A matrix \(A\) is diagonalizable if it can be written as
\[
A = V \Lambda V^{-1},
\] where the columns of \(V\) are the eigenvectors of \(A\) and \(\Lambda\) is a diagonal matrix containing the corresponding eigenvalues.
NB1: Not all matrices are diagonalizable. In such cases, we may need to consider generalized eigenvectors and the Jordan canonical form.
NB2: When \(A\) is symmetric, it is always diagonalizable with an orthonormal set of eigenvectors.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Why Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues Matter
Variational Interpretation:Eigenvectors and eigenvalues are solutions of optimization problems:
\[
\lambda_{\max}(A) = \max_{\mathbf{v} \neq 0} \frac{\mathbf{v}^\top A \mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{v}^\top \mathbf{v}}
\]
This can be generalized to other eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenvectors (see the Courant-Fischer min-max theorem in review notes).
Geometric Interpretation: Eigenvectors indicate directions in which the linear transformation associated with the matrix acts by simply scaling, and the corresponding eigenvalues indicate the scaling factor.
For a symmetric matrix \(A\): \[
A = Q \Lambda Q^\top = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \mathbf{q}_i \mathbf{q}_i^\top,
\] a weighted sum of projections onto the eigenvectors.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Why Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues Matter 2

Geometric Interpretation: Eigenvectors indicate directions in which the linear transformation associated with the matrix acts by simply scaling, and the corresponding eigenvalues indicate the scaling factor.
Algebraic Interpretation: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues provide a way to understand the structure of a matrix through its diagonalization, revealing invariant subspaces and simplifying matrix computations.
\[
A^t \mathbf{u} = Q \lambda^t Q^{-1} \mathbf{u}
\] This is super-useful for solving linear ODEs: \[
\mathbf{\dot{x}}(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t) \to
\mathbf{x}(t) = e^{At} \mathbf{x}(0) = Q e^{\Lambda t} Q^{-1} \mathbf{x}(0).
\]

Differential operators, Chebyshev / Fourier bases

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
A random surfer
Web = directed graph \(G=(V,E)\). The surfer follows a random out-link, but with probability \(1-\alpha\) teleports to a uniformly random page:
\[
M \;=\; \alpha P + (1-\alpha)\,\tfrac1n \mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top .
\]

The PageRank vector is a left eigenvector with eigenvalue 1:
\[
\pi^\top M = \pi^\top .
\]


Perron–Frobenius: \(M\) is strictly positive and stochastic, so \(\pi\) exists, is unique, and is entrywise positive.

§1 total ~12 min. Perron–Frobenius (informal): strictly positive irreducible matrix ⇒ real, simple, largest-modulus eigenvalue with positive eigenvector.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
section: The algorithm is the eigenvector computation
text:
The algorithm is the eigenvector computation
Power iteration: \(\;\pi_{k+1}^\top = \pi_k^\top M\).

Why it converges: teleportation is a contraction in \(\ell_1\). A difference of probability vectors sums to \(0\), so the teleport term drops out:
\[
\|\pi_{k+1} - \pi\|_1 = \alpha\,\big\|(\pi_k - \pi)^\top P\big\|_1 \;\le\; \alpha\,\|\pi_k - \pi\|_1,\\
\qquad\text{so}\qquad \|\pi_k - \pi\|_1 \le 2\,\alpha^k .
\]
Spectrally: \[\;\operatorname{spec}(M) = \{1\} \cup \alpha\cdot\{\lambda_2(P),\dots,\lambda_n(P)\},\] so the spectral gap is \(1 - |\lambda_2(M)| \ge 1 - \alpha\).



Discussion: what does a small spectral gap mean physically for the surfer?


Answer: slow mixing — the surfer’s distribution takes a long time to forget where it started. Same phenomenon as Markov chain mixing time; formalized with graph spectral gaps in a few weeks.
Contraction proof: for probability vectors \(x,y\), \(z = x-y\) has \(z^\top\mathbf 1 = 0\), so \(z^\top M = \alpha z^\top P + \tfrac{1-\alpha}{n}(z^\top\mathbf 1)\mathbf 1^\top = \alpha z^\top P\); \(P\) row-stochastic gives \(\|z^\top P\|_1 \le \|z\|_1\). Apply with \(x = \pi_k\), \(y = \pi\).
Eigenvalue proof (Haveliwala–Kamvar 2003): if \(x^\top M = \lambda x^\top\) with \(\lambda \ne 1\), then \(M\mathbf 1 = \mathbf 1\) forces \(x^\top\mathbf 1 = 0\), hence \(x^\top P = (\lambda/\alpha)x^\top\), so \(|\lambda| \le \alpha\). Equality iff \(P\) has a second unimodular eigenvalue (e.g. two closed components). Assumes dangling pages are patched so \(P\) is row-stochastic.
Why prefer the contraction: \(M\) is non-normal, so the eigenvalue bound only gives \(C|\lambda_2(M)|^k\) with \(C\) depending on eigenvector conditioning; the \(\ell_1\) argument has constant 1 and holds for every \(k\). That is the dashed \(\alpha^k\) line in the demo. Well-mixed graph: \(|\lambda_2(P)|\) small, so the error beats \(\alpha^k\) by a lot; two communities: \(\lambda_2(P) \approx 1\), error tracks \(\alpha^k\).

title: Why Eigenvectors?
section: A remark to flag now, pay off later
text:
A remark to flag now, pay off later
\(M\) comes from a directed graph, so it is generally

not symmetric,
not even normal (\(MM^* \neq M^*M\)),
with left and right eigenvectors that differ.

No inner product makes it self-adjoint: no diagonal reweighting enforces detailed balance on a generic directed graph.

Perron–Frobenius still gives a real, positive dominant eigenvalue — but the clean orthogonal-eigenbasis picture of the spectral theorem is not operating here.


Hold that thought — it resurfaces in §2, in reverse.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Partitioning a graph
Weighted undirected graph, adjacency \(A\), degrees \(D\), Laplacian
\[
L = D - A, \qquad x^\top L x = \sum_{(i,j)\in E} w_{ij}(x_i - x_j)^2 \;\ge 0, \qquad L\mathbf 1 = 0 .
\]

Goal: clusters with few crossing edges (Conductance/Normalized Cut Objective). NP-hard as stated.


Relax the \(\pm1\) indicator to any real vector:
\[
\min_{\mathbf{x}^\top D\mathbf 1 = 0}\; \frac{\mathbf{x}^\top L \mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{x}^\top D \mathbf{x}} \;=\; \lambda_2(L),
\]
attained exactly by the Fiedler vector \(v_2\).

§2 total ~15 min. The Rayleigh quotient on the board: extrema over the unit sphere are the extreme eigenvalues; Courant–Fischer gives the rest.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:

Start in “True layout”. Then “Scrambled” — the algorithm never saw the geometry, only the edges; colors still separate the blobs. Then “Ordered by Fiedler”. Increase bridge weight / count: λ₂ grows, the gap to λ₃ closes, clustering gets worse. The Cheeger readout at the bottom previews §3.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Self-adjointness, precisely
For any undirected weighted graph (no regularity needed):

\(L_{rw} = D^{-1}L\) and \(P = D^{-1}A\) are self-adjoint w.r.t. \(\langle x,y\rangle_D = x^\top D y\) — this is exactly detailed balance for \(\pi \propto \deg\);
\(\mathcal L = D^{1/2} L_{rw} D^{-1/2}\) is the same operator, self-adjoint w.r.t. the standard inner product.



A change of which inner product you measure against — not a repair of a broken operator. Undirected graphs get this for free; directed graphs (§1) generally do not.


This is Exercise 4 in the Linear Algebra Review note — assign before or after this lecture.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
An eigenvalue certifies a bottleneck
Conductance of \(G\): \[
h(G) = \min_{S}\; \frac{|\partial S|}{\min\big(\mathrm{vol}(S),\, \mathrm{vol}(V\setminus S)\big)} .
\]

Cheeger’s inequality. With \(\lambda_2\) the second-smallest eigenvalue of \(\mathcal L\),
\[
\frac{\lambda_2}{2} \;\le\; h(G) \;\le\; \sqrt{2\lambda_2} .
\]



Not a heuristic: a two-sided, provable certificate.
The upper bound is constructive: a sweep cut of \(D^{-1/2}v_2\) achieves it (the dashed line in the demo).
Proof later in the term; then SDP relaxations (ARV) and sparsification (Spielman–Teng).


~10 min. Goal today is the shape of the result, not the proof. Fill in the week number for the proof.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
The spectral theorem
PCA computes eigenvectors of the (symmetric, PSD) covariance matrix. Time to state what §2–3 were quietly leaning on:

Spectral theorem. If \(A = A^*\) on an \(n\)-dimensional inner product space, there is an orthonormal basis \(v_1,\dots,v_n\) of eigenvectors with real eigenvalues: \[A = Q\Lambda Q^*, \qquad Q \text{ unitary}.\]


SVD is the rectangular generalization: \(A = U\Sigma V^*\).
Eckart–Young. \(A_k = \sum_{i\le k} \sigma_i u_i v_i^*\) is the best rank-\(k\) approximation in Frobenius and operator norm: \(\;\|A - A_k\|_F^2 = \sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2 .\)

§4 total ~12 min. This is the result every student has used via sklearn without knowing it’s a spectral-theorem statement dressed up.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
The framing line

“Every example so far that behaved nicely — orthogonal eigenvectors, real eigenvalues, stable numerics — was secretly symmetric, or could be made symmetric. PageRank’s matrix was not, and we saw the clean picture partially break. Much of this course is about knowing which case you’re in before you start computing.”

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Heat on a graph
\[
\frac{du}{dt} = -Lu,\quad u(0)=u_0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
u(t) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\,\langle u_0, v_k\rangle\, v_k .
\]


\(\lambda_1 = 0\): the constant mode survives forever (equilibrium).
Every other mode decays at its own rate \(e^{-\lambda_k t}\).
The slowest non-constant mode is \(v_2\) — the Fiedler vector again.




Same eigenvector, two jobs: “the best 2-way cut” and “the last non-uniform heat left before equilibrium.”


§5 total ~12–15 min. Loosely follows the opening of Rosenberg, The Laplacian on a Riemannian Manifold. Qualitative today.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:

open in new tab ↗



Cycle first: press Play; the blue curve is the continuous heat kernel on a circle of the same length (Fourier eigenbasis) — discrete and continuous agree once the high modes are gone. Then “Two clusters + bridge”: after the high modes die, what remains is exactly the orange Fiedler mode — one cluster warm, the other cool. Path: slowest of all (λ₂ ≈ π²/n²).

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
From graphs to manifolds
Replace the graph by a compact Riemannian manifold \((M,g)\) and \(L\) by the Laplace–Beltrami operator \(\Delta = -\operatorname{div}\operatorname{grad}\):

self-adjoint, \(\Delta \succeq 0\), discrete spectrum \(0 = \lambda_1 < \lambda_2 \le \cdots \to \infty\);
eigenfunctions \(\phi_k\) form an orthonormal basis of \(L^2(M)\).


Heat equation \(\partial_t u = -\Delta u\), solved by the heat kernel
\[
K(t,x,y) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\,\phi_k(x)\,\phi_k(y).
\]
The same equation as the graph case — a finite sum becomes a discrete-but-infinite one.

The eigenbasis comes from Theorem 7.1 in Linear Algebra Review, Part II (see its Section 8), applied to the compact self-adjoint resolvent (I+Δ)⁻¹.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Where the geometry hides
Heat trace, as \(t \to 0^+\) (Minakshisundaram–Pleijel):
\[
Z(t) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t} \;\sim\; (4\pi t)^{-n/2}\Big(\mathrm{Vol}(M) + \tfrac{t}{6}\!\int_M \mathrm{Scal}\,dV + O(t^2)\Big).
\]
From the list of eigenvalues alone you read off:

the dimension \(n\) (rate of blow-up),
the volume (leading coefficient),
the total scalar curvature (next coefficient).


Weyl’s law, from the other end: \[N(\lambda) = \#\{k: \lambda_k \le \lambda\} \;\sim\; \frac{\omega_n \mathrm{Vol}(M)}{(2\pi)^n}\,\lambda^{n/2}.\]

title: Why Eigenvectors?
section: Can one hear the shape of a drum?
text:
Can one hear the shape of a drum?


Kac (1966): a drum’s shape determines its frequencies. Can you run that backward?

Gordon–Webb–Wolpert (1992): no. Two non-isometric planar drums with identical spectra.



The spectrum determines a great deal (dimension, volume, curvature, bottlenecks, …) — but not everything. Where exactly the line falls is a theme we return to.



Either way, actually computing with a continuous operator like \(\Delta\) is a real numerical problem. →

“Spectral” for eigenvalue problems comes from the analogy with spectral lines in physics.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Same word, different community
Solve \(\;u'' = e^{4x}\) on \([-1,1]\), \(\;u(\pm1)=0\).

Finite differences: local stencils, error \(O(N^{-2})\).
Chebyshev collocation: global polynomial basis, error \(O(\rho^{-N})\) for smooth \(u\) — “spectral” convergence.



§6 ~15 min. The intended “wow”: ~20 Chebyshev points reach machine precision; finite differences with thousands of points are still around 1e-6. Mention Orr–Sommerfeld (next slide) as a name-drop.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Planting a seed: non-normal operators
The Orr–Sommerfeld operator (hydrodynamic stability) is not self-adjoint.

Eigenvalues alone can badly mislead about its behavior.
Transient growth, sensitivity to perturbation → pseudospectra.


Same warning as PageRank, now for differential operators. We return to this once we have the machinery.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
section: Spherical harmonics and the global forecast
text:
Spherical harmonics and the global forecast
Operational global forecasting has long used the spectral transform method: expand fields in spherical harmonics (eigenfunctions of \(\Delta\) on \(S^2\)).

Smooth global fields ⇒ exponential convergence (as in §6).
A modest number of degrees of freedom buys enormous accuracy.


Not a classroom curiosity: part of why a global forecast is computationally tractable at all.


~5 min. Currency check before lecture: confirm current operational models’ numerics before citing specifics (e.g. ECMWF IFS), since this has been an active area of change.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Roadmap for the semester

Spectral graph theory proper: expanders, mixing times, Cheeger’s inequality (proved).
Spectral algorithms in ML: clustering, embeddings, low-rank models, diffusion maps.
The recurring question underneath all of it:


What do we actually need — self-adjointness, normality, or just diagonalizability — and what breaks when we don’t have it?

PageRank and directed graphs were today’s first data point. More will come.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Operators and the spectral theorem
Inner product / adjoint. On \(\mathbb F^n\), \(\langle x,y\rangle = y^*x\). The adjoint satisfies \(\langle Ax,y\rangle = \langle x,A^*y\rangle\). \(A\) is self-adjoint if \(A=A^*\); normal if \(AA^* = A^*A\) (orthonormal eigenbasis, possibly complex eigenvalues).
Spectral theorem. \(A=A^*\) on an \(n\)-dim inner product space ⇒ orthonormal eigenbasis, real eigenvalues \(\lambda_1\ge\dots\ge\lambda_n\); \(A = Q\Lambda Q^*\).
Rayleigh quotient. \(R_A(x) = \langle Ax,x\rangle / \langle x,x\rangle\); extrema on the unit sphere are the extreme eigenvalues (Courant–Fischer gives the rest).
Perron–Frobenius (informal). Strictly positive irreducible matrix ⇒ real, simple, largest-in-modulus eigenvalue with a strictly positive eigenvector.
SVD / Eckart–Young. \(A = U\Sigma V^*\); \(A_k = \sum_{i\le k}\sigma_i u_i v_i^*\) is the best rank-\(k\) approximation in Frobenius and operator norm.

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Graphs
For \(G=(V,E,w)\) undirected, symmetric adjacency \(A\), \(D = \mathrm{diag}(\deg)\):

\(L = D - A\): symmetric, PSD, \(\mathbf 1\in\ker L\).
\(L_{rw} = D^{-1}L\), \(\;P = D^{-1}A\).
\(\mathcal L = D^{-1/2}LD^{-1/2} = I - D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}\).

Degree-weighted inner product \(\langle x,y\rangle_D = x^\top D y\): \(L_{rw}\) and \(P\) are self-adjoint w.r.t. it; \(\mathcal L = D^{1/2}L_{rw}D^{-1/2}\) is self-adjoint w.r.t. the standard one.
Conductance \(h(G) = \min_S |\partial S| / \min(\mathrm{vol}(S),\mathrm{vol}(V\setminus S))\). Cheeger: \(\lambda_2(\mathcal L)/2 \le h(G) \le \sqrt{2\lambda_2(\mathcal L)}\).
Heat semigroup. \(u(t) = e^{-tL}u_0 = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\langle u_0,v_k\rangle v_k\); kernel \(K_t = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}v_kv_k^\top\).

title: Why Eigenvectors?
text:
Manifolds and numerics
Laplace–Beltrami. On compact \((M,g)\), \(\Delta = -\operatorname{div}\operatorname{grad}\) is self-adjoint, \(\Delta\succeq0\), spectrum \(0=\lambda_1<\lambda_2\le\cdots\to\infty\), eigenfunctions \(\phi_k\) an ONB of \(L^2(M)\). Heat kernel \(K(t,x,y) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\phi_k(x)\phi_k(y)\).
Heat trace. \(Z(t) = \operatorname{Tr} e^{-t\Delta} \sim (4\pi t)^{-n/2}\big(\mathrm{Vol}(M) + \tfrac t6\int_M \mathrm{Scal}\,dV + O(t^2)\big)\).
Weyl’s law. \(N(\lambda) \sim \dfrac{\omega_n\mathrm{Vol}(M)}{(2\pi)^n}\lambda^{n/2}\).
Spectral convergence. For smooth data, global (Chebyshev/Fourier) bases converge faster than any power of \(1/N\); local finite-difference stencils converge at a fixed polynomial rate.
